digest.intro: Autonomy goes live in warfare, orbit, and the exam hall today.

items.title: US AI Gives Ukraine's Kamikaze Drones Autonomous Targeting
items.blurb: Starting mid-July, Ukraine's $400 Shrike FPV drones began shipping with Auterion's Skynode S kit — 50,000 units contracted — letting an operator fly to a target area, flip a switch, and let the drone lock on and terminal-guide itself even through full radio jamming. The doctrine shift is subtle but seismic: the human is now optional at the moment of kill. Swarm autonomy (Nemyx) is already in testing, which is where this obviously goes next.

items.title: SpaceX to Acquire 130,000 Acres of Louisiana Marshland
items.blurb: An 18-mile Gulf Coast stretch at Pecan Island, freed up by an ExxonMobil pollution settlement, is about to become SpaceX territory — the company targeting thousands of Starship flights per year needs its own sovereign-ish launch geography, not just range time. Louisiana sweetened the deal with liability protections and property tax breaks passed earlier this year. This is less a real estate story than a preview of what private infrastructure at planetary scale looks like.

items.title: Trump Wants Power to Block Citizens from Suing Polluters
items.blurb: Since the 1970s, citizen suit provisions in the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, and Safe Drinking Water Act have produced over 2,000 lawsuits — the majority of all environmental enforcement cases. The DOJ is now arguing, in a case involving Elon Musk's xAI, that citizens should be barred from enforcing those laws even when the executive chooses not to act. The mechanism being dismantled isn't a technicality; it's the entire non-governmental check on industrial pollution.

items.title: Trump's AI Protectionism Has Come for Robotics
items.blurb: The FTC just issued a sweeping ban on foreign-made advanced robots — humanoids, quadrupeds, wheeled platforms — citing both data-security risk and the need to protect nascent US manufacturers from cheap Chinese competition. It follows the same playbook used against solar panels, EVs, and drones, but this time it lands on a sector that barely exists yet at commercial scale. The effect is to make US robotics industrial policy out of a still-stumbling technology.

items.title: LLMs Reward Expertise
items.blurb: The piece uses Terence Tao's actual ChatGPT conversation about a new Jacobian Conjecture counterexample as evidence: Tao's messages are terse and expert-signaling, the model's responses are correspondingly dense and concise — a completely different register than what a layperson gets from the same model. The argument is that LLMs don't flatten the gap between novice and expert; they amplify it, because expertise is what unlocks the model's best mode. Useful framing for anyone wondering what skill looks like in an AI-saturated field.

items.title: An AI-Supervised Exam Went So Badly That 58,000 Students Must Retake It
items.blurb: Mexico's UNAM ran its 160,000-applicant entrance exam remotely for the first time, with AI webcam proctoring — and top scores (110+/120) increased 6x over the previous five-year average. An expert commission concluded the only credible path forward is an in-person re-exam for all 58,000 who would have been admitted going back to 2021. It's a clean case study in what institutional collapse by AI-enabled cheating actually looks like at scale.

items.title: MiniMax H3: Open-Weights 2K Video with Native Audio, Day-0 in ComfyUI
items.blurb: MiniMax H3 dropped with open weights and same-day ComfyUI support — text, image, video, or audio in; 2K video with real stereo audio (generated in the same pass, not bolted on) out, up to 15 seconds, reportedly runnable on a 3060. The first-and-last-frame and reference-to-video modes are the interesting creative controls: lock the opening and closing frames, let the model solve the middle. Worth pulling in today if you want to test what the open-weights video ceiling looks like right now.

items.title: Ella & Pitr: Murals Made to Be Seen from the Air
items.blurb: Ella & Pitr paint enormous figures across rooftops, playing fields, and parking lots — images that only fully cohere from an altitude the artists cannot occupy while making them. The constraint is doing real conceptual work: you're composing for a viewpoint you'll never inhabit during production, which is a strange and interesting inversion of the usual maker-to-audience relationship. Their upcoming show at Galerie Jonathan Roze in Rennes is called Points de Suspension.

items.title: Is Spider Web Really Stronger Than Steel?
items.blurb: Veritasium at his best: a question that sounds settled (yes, spider silk is stronger by weight) turns out to be full of counterintuitive physics once you ask what 'stronger' actually means and whether you could fabricate anything useful at scale. The rabbit hole leads into material science, biological fabrication limits, and the gap between tensile strength and toughness — the kind of narrow obsessive thing that makes you want to immediately look up dragline silk synthesis.

items.title: The Virtue of Being Simple
items.blurb: Sacculina barnacles begin life with a functioning brain, use it to find a crab host, then deliberately shed it — along with every other organ they no longer need — becoming essentially a root system with gonads. The evolutionary argument is rigorous: in a stable, solved environment, intelligence is metabolically expensive overhead, and the winning strategy is radical simplification. At a moment of maximum AI intelligence-worship, a well-evidenced case that more cognitive complexity is not always adaptive lands as genuine counterweight.

facts.fact: Between 2021–2025, only 0.9% of UNAM entrance exam takers scored 110 or higher; this year, under AI proctoring, 5.5% did — a 6x increase that triggered a mandatory re-exam for 58,000 people.

Ukraine's Auterion-equipped Shrike drones can autonomously track and strike a moving target up to half a mile away even after losing all radio contact with the human operator due to jamming or terrain.
SpaceX's 130,000-acre Louisiana site became available because it was part of a legal settlement resolving dozens of lawsuits blaming ExxonMobil for pollution and coastal land loss.

Since the 1970s, citizen suit provisions — which the Trump DOJ now argues should be eliminated — have produced over 2,000 environmental lawsuits and constitute the majority of all US environmental enforcement cases.

Sacculina barnacles literally shed their own brains upon finding a host, reverting from a sensory-capable larva to what researchers describe as 'a root system with gonads' — a deliberate evolutionary regression away from intelligence.

make_something.prompt: Ella & Pitr compose for a viewpoint they can't stand in while painting. Try the same constraint: design a piece — drawing, 3D scene, WebGL shader, anything — that only reads correctly from one specific external vantage point you define in advance but cannot occupy while making it. Could be a true anamorphic perspective, a rooftop layout only coherent in satellite view, or a generative piece that resolves into an image only when the camera hits an exact coordinate. The constraint is the work.

art_picks.title: Sans Soleil
art_picks.creator: Chris Marker
art_picks.why: A decades-long rabbit hole disguised as a travel essay — Marker builds a philosophy of memory, ritual, and image-making through the feedback loop between watcher and world. It will make you want to build something that thinks.

art_picks.title: Replica
art_picks.creator: Oneohtrix Point Never
art_picks.why: Lopatin treats old TV commercial samples as archaeological material — pulling emotional residue out of media detritus, looping them until they reveal the invisible systems that made them feel safe. Pure feedback-loop aesthetics with deep structural rigor.

art_picks.title: Flatland series / interactive installations
art_picks.creator: Casey Reas
art_picks.why: Reas encodes behavior rather than form — his systems generate images no single human decision could make, sitting exactly at the edge where software becomes self-expression and code becomes culture.

events.name: Whitney Biennial 2026 (82nd Edition)
events.venue: Whitney Museum of American Art, 99 Gansevoort St, Manhattan
events.why: 56 artists probing interspecies kinship, technological affinities, and shared mythologies — curators explicitly organized around 'relationality' and the hidden infrastructures of power; immersive video installations and technologically-driven works are standouts, and the closing date is Aug 23 so this is the last window.

events.name: It's Alive! A Century of Animation from the Collection
events.why: 200+ works tracing hand-drawn animation's NYC underground — from silent-era character logic to MTV-era experimental work to Sesame Street; a genealogy of expressive systems built frame by frame, deeply tied to the city's scene history.

events.name: Lily van der Stokker: Male Art Exhibition, Great Show
events.why: Van der Stokker's work is all playful surface concealing pointed critique of art-world status systems and gender — the title alone is a trap; she's been doing this category-subversion longer and weirder than almost anyone.

events.name: Summer Group Show (opening)
events.why: A small TriBeCa gallery with a track record of showing painters working at the edge of abstraction and representation — worth catching fresh on opening week before the summer crowd thins out further.

events.name: Midsummer Nights: Strings N' Skins
events.venue: Lincoln Place (Brooklyn Conservatory of Music), Brooklyn
events.why: Curated by Melanie Charles, this free open-air jazz series deliberately ignores genre walls — Strings N' Skins is an outdoor evening that turns a residential block into a listening room, exactly the kind of small-scene ritual that's visible before it hardens.
